Abstract The thermolysis reactions of benzoazacyclodecatrienes un-
der microwave irradiation conditions in toluene at 150 °C afforded com-
plex azabenzo[ a]cyclopropa[cd]azulene and (epiminomethano)cyclo-
penta[a]indene frameworks. Cyclopropanes were established as
intermediates of the ultimate thermolysis products.
Key words thermal transformation, azacyclic allene, cyclopropanes,
epiminomethanocyclopentaindenes, microwave-assisted reaction,
polyheterocyclic compounds
In recent years, microwave irradiation has been widely
applied in the synthesis of heterocyclic compounds, includ-
ing polycyclic nitrogen-containing derivatives.
1–3 These ap-
proaches permit the efficient formation of structurally
complex compounds that are interesting for their natural
origin or their biological activity.
3–5 In this work, to increase
the accessibility of complex frameworks, we proposed to
use the thermal rearrangement of cyclic allenes containing
an enamine fragment.
Synthetic methods for transformations of cyclic allenes,
particularly those containing a heteroatom, remain largely
unstudied. In selected examples, [2,3]- and [3,3]-sigma-
tropic rearrangements are crucial for the formation of het-
erocyclic allenes and their thermal transformation products
(Scheme 1). In this manner, azacyclononatrienes 1 were ob-
tained in low yields (30–40%) from 6-ethynyl-1-car-
boxymethyl-1,2,5,6-tetrahydropyridinium salts in the pres-
ence of DBU
6 (Scheme 1).
The same authors applied this method to a moderate-
yielding construction of the sulfur-containing nonacyclic
allenes 2 from the corresponding 1-alkynyl-2-(2-ethoxy-
carbonyl)-3,4-dihydro-1H-isothiochromenium triflates in
the presence of DBU. 7 Lactams such as the 3-chloro-1-aza-
deca- and -undeca-4,5-diene-2-ones 3 were obtained

through a [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement of 2-(phenyl-
ethynyl)-N-methylpiperidine or -azepine, respectively, with
chloroacetyl fluoride.8 Our research group has also reported
a synthesis of 8-substituted benzazecines 4 containing an
allene moiety from 1-substituted 1-(phenylethynyl)-
1,2,3,4-tetrahydroisoquinolines and electron-deficient
alkynes (Scheme 1).
9
These first steps taken in obtaining cyclic allenes con-
taining a ring heteroatom have permitted us to begin study-
ing the properties of these compounds. Dimerization or in-
termolecular cycloaddition result in carbocycles in a reac-
tion that is a characteristic chemical property of cyclic
allenes.
10–12 The direction of this interaction is often deter-
mined by the temperature at which the reaction occurs
(Scheme 2, upper). However, there is only one example of a
thermal isomerization of a heterocyclic allene: the transfor-
mation of 1,2,4,-trihydro-3-benzothionines 2 into the cor-
responding 1,3-diene structures 6 (Scheme 2, lower).
7
Scheme 2  Examples of thermal transformations of cyclic allenes
Our goal was to study the thermal transformation of
azacyclic allenes 4a–e (Table 1) and the effects of substitu-
ents on the thermolysis of these compounds. Azacyclodeca-
trienes 4a, 4c, and 4e have been previously obtained by the
reaction of the corresponding 1-(phenylethynyl)isoquino-
lines with methyl propiolate in trifluoroethanol at 7 °C
(Scheme 1):
9 compounds 4b and 4d are novel. 13 Initially,
benzoazacyclodecatrienes 4a–e were heated in toluene un-
der microwave irradiation conditions [150 °C, 30 min; see
Supporting Information (SI) and Procedure A]
14 to give mix-
tures of 2-azabenzo[ a]cyclopropa[cd]azulenes 7a–e and
(epiminomethano)cyclopenta[a]indenes 8a–e. Prolonged
heating of azacyclic allenes 4a–e in toluene under micro-
wave irradiation caused the reaction to proceed to comple-
tion, yielding the (epiminomethano)cyclopenta[ a]indenes
8a–e exclusively. During this thermolysis process, monitor-
ing by thin-layer chromatography showed that the starting
allene 4 and cyclopropane 7 disappeared as indene 8 ap-
peared. We therefore suggest that the cyclopropanes 7a–e
were the primary thermolysis products, and that further
heating in toluene led to the formation of indenes 8a–e (Ta-
ble 1; see also SI and Procedure B).
15
Table 1  Thermolysis of Allenes 4a–e
The higher yields of the cyclopropane-containing het-
erocycles 7a and 7e with a methyl group at the C-4b posi-
tion indicate that these compounds are more stable than
the 2-azabenzo[ a]cyclopropa[cd]azulene 7d substituted
with a phenyl group on the same atom, which exhibits
greater reactivity in the observed thermal rearrangements
(Table 1).
The thermolysis products where formed as single dia-
stereoisomers, i.e., 7 and 8.
16 We confirmed the structures of
compounds 7 and 8 by 1H NMR spectroscopic analysis,
which that showed the presence of single sets of signals.

It is well known that allenes can be excited to form a bi-
radical A that undergoes skeletal rearrangement. 18–20 Be-
cause the rearrangement of compounds 4 occurred upon
heating to 150 °C, a radical mechanism can be presumed.
We therefore assume that the reaction mechanism starts
with formation of biradical intermediate A (Scheme 3).
21 In
the next stage, hydrogen migration occurs from the benzyl
CH
2-group to the C-7 carbon, and the cyclopropane ring 7 is
formed via intermediates B and C. Further heating of the cy-
clopropane derivative results in its transformation into
product 8 via biradical D.
We experimentally established that heating the isolated
compound 7a (R = OMe; R
1 = Me) gave product 8a in 50%
yield (SI and Procedure C).22 This rearrangement leading to
the thermodynamically more stable product 8a with a cy-
clopentene moiety, can be considered as a retro-reaction of
the cyclopropane-containing compound 7a through C–C
bond cleavage of a three-membered ring. A similar transfor-

In summary, the thermal transformations of ben-
zazecines containing enamine and allene moieties leading
to azabenzo[ a]cyclopropa[cd]azulenes 7 and (epimino-
methano)cyclopenta[a]indenes 8 was examined. The azu-

sis of the indenes 8.

(15) General Procedure A
A solution of the appropriate allene derivative (0.68 mmol) in
dry toluene (6.0 mL) was placed in a microwave reactor and
heated at 150 °C for 30 min while the progress of the reaction
was monitored by TLC [EtOAc–hexane, 1:1 ( 4a and 4c); EtOAc–
hexane, 1:2 ( 4b, 4d, and 4e)]. The solvent was evaporated in
vacuo. Products 7a–c, 7e, and 8a–e were isolated by chromatog-
raphy on silica gel; compounds 7a and 7c, 7b and 8b, 7e, 8a, 8c,
and 8e were eluted with EtOAc–hexane (1:3, 1:5, 1:12, 1:2, 1:1,
and 1:10, respectively).
(16) General Procedure B
A solution of the appropriate allene derivative (0.16 mmol) in
dry toluene (6.0 mL) was irradiated in a microwave reactor at
150 °C for 3–7.5 h with stirring while the progress of the reac-
tion was monitored by TLC [EtOAc–hexane, 1:1 ( 4a and 4c);
EtOAc–hexane, 1:2, ( 4b, 4d, and 4e)]. The solvent was evapo-
rated in vacuo and products 8a–e were crystallized from Et
2O.
